How often should you wash your car in a New Brunswick winter?

Short answer: after every storm once the roads are salted, and at least every week or two through salt season, with an underbody flush.

From the first snowfall until the street sweepers come out in spring, the roads around Quispamsis, Rothesay and Saint John are treated with salt and brine. It keeps the roads drivable. It also coats every car that drives on them, and most of it ends up where you can't see it.

Why salt is worth washing off

Salt on its own does little. Salt plus moisture speeds up rust on any bare or chipped metal, and winter here is wet: slush, freeze and thaw cycles, and the salt fog that rolls in off the Bay of Fundy. A crust that sits on your car for weeks keeps working the whole time, especially on mild days when it turns back into salty water.

Where salt does the most damage

  • Brake and fuel lines run along the underside, right in the spray from your tires.
  • Rocker panels and door bottoms catch slush thrown up from the road.
  • Wheel wells pack with salty slush that can sit there for days.
  • The exhaust and subframe are bare or lightly coated metal.
  • Paint chips on the hood and around the wheel arches are where rust starts on the body.

How often to wash

A good rule for a Maritime winter:

  • After every storm, once the roads have been salted and the main roads are clear.
  • Every week or two in between, even if the car looks fine. Brine dries to a thin grey film that's easy to miss.
  • On milder days when you can. Washing above freezing means less chance of doors and locks icing up afterward.
  • One last thorough wash in spring to get the season's salt out of the underbody before summer.

What kind of wash

In winter the underbody matters more than the shine. A wash with an underbody flush rinses salt from the places a hose or a wand can't reach, and doing it in a heated tunnel beats standing in the driveway at minus ten. At Wash 66 the underbody flush with rust inhibitor is part of the Better and Best washes.

Cold-day tips after a wash

  • Open and close each door once so the seals don't freeze shut.
  • Wipe the door seals and the edges of the mirrors with a dry towel.
  • If it's well below freezing, drive a few minutes with the heat on before you park for the night.

Making it easy

Washing after every storm adds up quickly if you pay each time. A monthly membership lets you wash once a day for one price, so a salty week costs nothing extra. Most visits take about two minutes, and the covered vacuum bays are there for salt-stained floor mats.
